schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Extract from the filename using regex pattern 'Pd[_ ]?n(\d+)' to capture the sample number. Example: '20251125Pdn7-CV-10mVperSecond.txt' → match 'Pdn7' → extract '7' → construct 'Pd n7'. Step 2: If the pattern does not match, try alternative patterns: 'Pd[_ ]?(\d+)', 'Pd_n(\d+)', 'Pdn(\d+)' (case-insensitive). Step 3: If still no match, look for 'sample' or 'id' keywords in the file header or metadata section. Step 4: Store the extracted sample_id string in the format 'Pd nX' where X is the number. Do NOT leave null or invent a value. If no sample identifier is found in filename or header, set to null.
schema_fields.description: Unique identifier for the sample (e.g., 'Pd n7', 'Pd n6', 'Pd n114')
schema_fields.name: sample_id

schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Extract from filename using regex pattern: '-(\d+)mVperSecond\.txt$' or '_(\d+)mV[_/]?s'. Example: '20251125Pdn7-CV-5mVperSecond.txt' → extract '5' → store as number 5.0. Step 2: If filename does not match, calculate from time-series data: call query_timeseries(column='<potential_column>', operation='diff') to get potential differences, call query_timeseries(column='time (s)' or similar, operation='diff') to get time differences. Compute scan_rate = mean(abs(potential_diff / time_diff)) * 1000 (convert V/s to mV/s). Step 3: Store the numeric result. Do NOT leave null or invent if either filename or time-series data is available.
schema_fields.description: Scan rate in mV/s for cyclic voltammetry or linear sweep voltammetry experiments
schema_fields.name: scan_rate_mv_per_s

schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Identify the current column (e.g., 'WE(1).Current (A)') and potential column (e.g., 'Potential applied (V)' or 'WE(1).Potential (V)') from the file header. Step 2: Call query_timeseries(column='<potential_column>', operation='values') to get the full potential array. Step 3: Call query_timeseries(column='<current_column>', operation='values') to get the full current array. Step 4: Divide the potential range into segments (e.g., 0.05 V windows). For each segment, compute the standard deviation of current values within that potential window. Step 5: Identify the potential range where the current standard deviation is minimal (typically the lowest 20-30% of observed std values across all segments), indicating flat, capacitive-only response. Step 6: Store the result as a string in the format 'min_potential to max_potential V' (e.g., '-0.003 to 0.400 V'). Do NOT leave null or invent. Base the range solely on the statistical analysis of current variance across potential.
schema_fields.description: Potential range (in volts) where capacitive (non-faradaic) current dominates, typically characterized by featureless current response
schema_fields.name: capacitive_region_potential_range

schema_fields.comment: Extract from the file header or column name containing 'Current'. Look for unit specification in parentheses, e.g., 'WE(1).Current (A)' → extract 'A'. schema_fields.description: Unit of measurement for current (e.g., A, mA, µA, or normalized units such as A/cm²)
schema_fields.name: current_unit

schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Identify the potential column name from the file header (e.g., 'Potential applied (V)' or 'WE(1).Potential (V)'). Step 2: Call query_timeseries(column='<potential_column>', operation='turning_points') to get indices of local minima and maxima. Step 3: Count the number of complete cycles: cycle_count = (number_of_turning_points - 1) / 2. Round down to nearest integer. Store the result. Do NOT leave null or invent.
schema_fields.description: Total number of complete cyclic voltammetry cycles in the dataset, determined by counting potential turning points (local minima and maxima)
schema_fields.name: cycle_count

schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Extract cycle_stability_coefficient_of_variation and cycle_count. Step 2: If cycle_count < 3, set to 'insufficient_cycles'. Step 3: If CV < 0.05, set to 'stable'. If 0.05 <= CV <= 0.10, set to 'moderately_stable'. If CV > 0.10, set to 'unstable'. Do NOT leave null or invent.
schema_fields.description: Qualitative assessment of cycle stability: 'stable' if coefficient of variation < 0.05 (5%), 'moderately_stable' if 0.05-0.10, 'unstable' if > 0.10, or 'insufficient_cycles' if fewer than 3 cycles
schema_fields.name: cycle_stability_assessment

schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Identify current column (e.g., 'WE(1).Current (A)') and potential column. Step 2: Use query_timeseries to segment data by cycles (via turning_points on potential). Step 3: For each cycle, compute integrated absolute charge: call query_timeseries(column='<current_column>', operation='integrate', filter={'cycle_index': i}) for each cycle i. Step 4: Compute mean and std of charge values across cycles. Step 5: Calculate CV = std / mean. Store the numeric result. If only 1 cycle, set to null. Do NOT invent.
schema_fields.description: Coefficient of variation (CV = std/mean) of integrated charge or peak current across all cycles, used to quantify cycle-to-cycle reproducibility. Lower values indicate better stability.
schema_fields.name: cycle_stability_coefficient_of_variation

schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Identify the current column (e.g., 'WE(1).Current (A)') and potential column from the file header. Step 2: Extract capacitive_region_potential_range to identify the potential window where capacitive current dominates. Step 3: For each scan rate in the dataset (from scan_rate_mv_per_s), call query_timeseries(column='<current_column>', operation='mean', filter={'potential_min': <capacitive_min>, 'potential_max': <capacitive_max>}) to get the average capacitive current in that region. Step 4: Plot capacitive current (A) vs. scan rate (V/s, convert mV/s to V/s by dividing by 1000). Step 5: Compute the slope of this linear relationship: slope = Δcurrent / Δscan_rate. Step 6: Convert slope to capacitance: C_dl (µF/cm²) = slope (A/(V/s)) / A_geometric (cm²) × 10^6 (to convert F to µF). If A_geometric is not available, store the slope in A/(V/s) and note that normalization is pending. Step 7: Store the numeric result in µF/cm². Do NOT leave null or invent. Base extraction solely on the linear fit of capacitive current vs. scan rate.
schema_fields.description: Double-layer capacitance C_dl in µF/cm², extracted from the slope of capacitive current vs. scan rate in the non-faradaic potential region
schema_fields.name: double_layer_capacitance_uf_cm2

schema_fields.description: Method used to calculate ECSA (e.g., 'hydrogen_upd_integration', 'double_layer_capacitance', 'other')
schema_fields.name: ecsa_calculation_method

schema_fields.comment: Step 1: Extract double_layer_capacitance_uf_cm2, specific_capacitance_uf_cm2, and geometric_electrode_area_cm2 from the schema. Step 2: If any of these fields are null, set ecsa_cm2 to null (cannot compute without all three values). Step 3: Compute ECSA using the formula: ECSA (cm²) = (C_dl (µF/cm²) × A_geometric (cm²)) / C_s (µF/cm²). Step 4: Store the numeric result in cm². Do NOT leave null or invent if all required fields are available. If the result is normalized per unit mass (e.g., cm²/g), note the normalization in the description.
schema_fields.description: Electrochemically active surface area in cm² or normalized units (cm²/g), typically derived from hydrogen adsorption/desorption charge integration
schema_fields.name: ecsa_cm2

Step 5: For each cycle, call query_timeseries(column='<current_column>', operation='integrate', filter={'start_index': turning_points[2*i], 'end_index': turning_points[2*i+2]}) to compute integrated charge. Step 3: For each scan rate in the dataset (from scan_rate_mv_per_s), call query_timeseries(column='<current_column>', operation='mean', filter={'potential_min': <capacitive_min>, 'potential_max': <capacitive_max>}) to get the average capacitive current in that region. Step 4: Plot capacitive current (A) vs. scan rate (V/s, convert mV/s to V/s by dividing by 1000). Step 5: Compute the slope of this linear relationship: slope = Δcurrent / Δscan_rate. Step 6: Convert slope to capacitance: C_dl (µF/cm²) = slope (A/(V/s)) / A_geometric (cm²) × 10^6 (to convert F to µF). If A_geometric is not available, store the slope in A/(V/s) and note that normalization is pending. Step 7: Store the numeric result in µF/cm². Do NOT leave null or invent. Step 1: Call query_timeseries(column='Delta L|d(µm/s)', operation='std') to get the standard deviation of the derivative. Step 2: Call query_timeseries(column='Delta L|d(µm/s)', operation='peaks') to identify spike locations. Step 3: Check if spikes correlate with features in Delta L(µm) by calling query_timeseries(column='Delta L(µm)', operation='derivative') and comparing. Step 4: If spikes are high-frequency (>3× std), random, and do NOT correspond to Delta L features, set false (instrumental). If spikes are smooth rate changes that match Delta L inflection points or phase transitions, set true (physical). In most dilatometry data, if smoothing_required_for_derivative=true, spikes are instrumental.
schema_fields.description: Whether derivative spikes in dL/dt are physical phenomena (true) or instrumental artifacts (false). Physical spikes represent real material responses: rapid hydrogen absorption/desorption events, phase transformation kinetics, or structural relaxation processes. These correlate with features in the Delta L(t) curve and are reproducible across replicate measurements. Instrumental spikes are measurement artifacts: electrical noise, mechanical vibrations, digitization errors, or sensor drift. These appear as random high-frequency fluctuations uncorrelated with the underlying dilatation trend and vary between replicates. In dilatometry, most high-frequency spikes in dL/dt that require smoothing are instrumental, while smooth rate changes reflecting Delta L features are physical.
